'''''Centaurea cineraria''''', the '''velvet centaurea''', also known as '''dusty miller''' and '''silver dust''' (though these latter two names may also apply to ''[[Jacobaea maritima]]'' and ''[[Silene coronaria]]''), is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Asteraceae]] [[endemism|endemic]] to southern [[Italy]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |title=Flora Europaea: Volume 4: Plantaginaceae to Compositae (and Rubiaceae) |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1976 |isbn=978-0-521-08717-9 |page=270}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Hind |first1=Nicholas |last2=Hashi |first2=Mayumi |last3=Brown |first3=Andrew |date=March 2022 |title=1009. CENTAUREA CINERARIA: Compositae |journal=Curtis's Botanical Magazine |language=en |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=35–54 |doi=10.1111/curt.12431 |s2cid=246185912 |issn=1355-4905|doi-access=free }}</ref> In natural settings, it grows on coastal cliffs, ranging from 0–350 m above sea level,<ref name=":1" /> hence the plant's Italian name, ''fiordaliso delle scogliere'' (lit. "cliff [[Centaurea|cornflower]]").<ref name=":1" />  Mature plants may reach {{convert|80|cm|in|1|round=0.5}} in height.<ref name=":0" /> The species produces purple flowers.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Centaurea in Flora of North America @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=106012 |access-date=2022-11-27 |website=www.efloras.org}}</ref><ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

''Centaurea cineraria'' is taxonomically complicated, with several described subspecies and significant geographic variation.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Domina |first1=Gianniantonio |last2=Greuter |first2=Werner |last3=Raimondo |first3=Francesco M. |date=2017-07-17 |title=A taxonomic reassessment of the Centaurea busambarensis complex (Compositae, Cardueae), with description of a new species from the Egadi Islands (W Sicily) |url=https://brill.com/view/journals/ijps/64/1-2/article-p48_5.xml |journal=Israel Journal of Plant Sciences |language=en |volume=64 |issue=1–2 |pages=48–56 |doi=10.1080/07929978.2016.1257146 |doi-broken-date=11 July 2025 |issn=0792-9978}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Guarino |first1=C. |last2=Salerno |first2=G. |last3=Cipriani |first3=G. |date=2013-12-01 |title=Effects of fragmentation phenomena on the genetic structure and gene flow in Centaurea cineraria group (Asteraceae) in the Mediterranean Basin |journal=Plant Biosystems |volume=147 |issue=4 |pages=996–1005 |doi=10.1080/11263504.2013.855276 |bibcode=2013PBios.147..996G |s2cid=83843344 |issn=1126-3504}}</ref> Members of the ''C. cineraria'' group have variously been treated as full species, as subspecies, or simply as regional variations.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":1" />

== In Horticulture ==
''Centaurea cineraria'' is commonly cultivated for its foliage.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Centaurea cineraria subsp. cineraria {{!}} dusty miller Bedding/RHS Gardening |url=http://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/75483/centaurea-cineraria-subsp-cineraria/details |access-date=2022-11-27 |website=www.rhs.org.uk |language=en-gb}}</ref> Depending on climate, it can be grown as either an annual or as a perennial. In cultivation, this species prefers full sun and well-drained soil.<ref name=":5" />

''Centaurea cineraria'' is sometimes referred to as ''[[Centaurea gymnocarpa]]'' within the horticultural trade, due to both taxonomic confusion and/or potential hybridization between ''C. cineraria'' and ''C. gymnocarpa'' in cultivation.<ref name=":1" /> However, cultivated material seems to mostly consist of ''C. cineraria'' in a narrower sense, with some possible introgression from other members of the ''C. cineraria'' group (including ''C. gymnocarpa'').<ref name=":1" /> True ''C. gymnocarpa'' is a rare plant in the wild and likely does not exist in cultivation outside of conservation settings.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=iucn>{{cite iucn |author=Foggi, B. |year=2006 |title=''Centaurea gymnocarpa'' |volume=2006 |article-number=e.T61620A12524846 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2006.RLTS.T61620A12524846.en |access-date=10 December 2024}}</ref> Despite past work that sometimes treated ''C. gymnocarpa'' as conspecific with ''C. cineraria'', current work supports both taxa at the species level.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite POWO | title=''Centaurea gymnocarpa'' Moris & De Not. | id=190613-1 |access-date=2022-11-27}}</ref><ref name=powo/><ref name=":3" />

''Centaurea cineraria'' occasionally escapes from cultivation, but, at least in North America, this has not resulted in established exotic populations.<ref name=":2" /> This species is, however, naturalized in [[New Zealand]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Flora of New Zealand {{!}} Taxon Profile {{!}} Centaurea cineraria |url=https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/taxon/Centaurea-cineraria.html |access-date=2023-02-14 |website=www.nzflora.info}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Centaurea cineraria |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/centaurea-cineraria/ |access-date=2023-02-14 |website=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |language=en}}</ref>

In the UK ''Centaurea cineraria'' subsp. ''cineraria'' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name="RHSPF">{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/75483/Centaurea-cineraria-subsp-cineraria/Details | title = ''Centaurea cineraria'' subsp. ''cineraria'' | website = www.rhs.org | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 12 April 2020}}</ref>

Because of similar leaf shape, leaf hairiness, and leaf color, there has been much confusion in the horticultural world between ''C. cineraria'' and the unrelated ''Jacobaea maritima'' (with ''Senecio cineraria'' being an old name for ''Jacobaea maritima'').<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite POWO |title=''Jacobaea maritima'' (L.) Pelser & Meijden |id=77075194-1 |access-date=2022-11-27}}</ref> ''Jacobaea maritima'' has similar foliage to ''C. cineraria'' ("cineraria" means "ash-gray colored").<ref name=":1" /> Cultivars like 'Silver Dust', 'Silver Lace', and 'Cirrus' are sometimes mistakenly referred to as ''C. cineraria'' but these cultivars actually pertain to ''J. maritima''.<ref name=":1" /> The cultivar 'Colchester White' (named for the leaf color, not the flower color) does actually pertain to ''C. cineraria'' and is the most common cultivar of this species.<ref name=":1" /> This confusion has also resulted in many images on the internet being mistakenly identified, resulting in identification of cultivated material challenging, especially without reproductive parts.<ref name=":1" />
